prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into the theory of international trade, and for showing how it shapes who exports, who invests abroad and how trade affects productivity and welfare

statement.case_for: The heterogeneous-firm framework moved trade analysis from countries and industries to firms. It explains exporter selection, within-industry reallocation and a gains-from-trade channel that earlier models lacked. Its predictions have been tested against firm-level microdata from many countries for more than twenty years, and the framework became a base for quantitative trade models and policy evaluation. Theory and evidence developed together, which is the combination I weigh most heavily. Attribution is relatively compact: Melitz is the originator, and Helpman co-developed the exporting-versus-FDI extension and the wider firm-level research programme. Trade has not been recognised since 2008, so timing is favourable. After reading colleagues' openings I still rank this first, though I treat it as a close call against B003 and B014.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and priority. Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum have parallel or antecedent claims on the empirical regularities and on related models, and they are not among the credited names. A Melitz-Helpman prize would therefore leave out part of the lineage. Krugman's 2008 prize also covers adjacent ground, so the citation must be framed carefully around selection and reallocation. Helpman is cross-listed in B030, which complicates how he is placed. Opening support is thinner than for B014 or B003: only four members ranked B047 in their top three. A majority is not obvious, and some of this is a real scientific doubt rather than a bargaining problem.

responses.point: Hassler ranks the Grossman-Helpman political economy of trade policy first. He sees a clean, long-standing two-person partnership, and he notes that trade's prior recognition is a timing risk rather than a confirmation risk.
responses.response: The attribution is indeed cleaner than in most candidates. Even so, I place B047 above B030 on empirical confirmation. Hassler himself notes that support for the protection-for-sale model is mixed across subfields, whereas the selection and reallocation predictions of the heterogeneous-firm model have been repeatedly confirmed in firm-level data. There is also a Helpman-placement problem: his claim in B047 rests on Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple and the firm-level programme, and his claim in B030 rests on a different body of work. I would not pursue both, and I think his strongest case in this cycle is with Melitz.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B014 first and B047 seventh. He worries that Krugman's 2008 prize overlaps with firm heterogeneity and that Bernard-Jensen empirical priority is not credited in the ballot names.
responses.response: I take the priority concern seriously, and I list it as a genuine uncertainty rather than dismissing it. On the overlap, Krugman's prize concerned scale economies, product differentiation and trade patterns. Selection into exporting and the productivity-reallocation channel are a different margin, and Strömberg and Friberg make the same distinction. Bernard and Jensen documented the exporter premia, but Melitz supplied the general-equilibrium model that turned them into a welfare and policy framework. The Committee has previously rewarded model-and-evidence combinations of this kind. The omitted names remain a cost, and I would want the citation to describe the theoretical framework rather than claim the whole empirical lineage. On B014, I agree with Krusell on its scientific stature. My doubt is attribution: the eleven proposed trios draw on Taylor, Woodford, Calvo and Gali in different combinations. That pattern suggests the Committee has no stable trio, and the omissions of Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets and Gertler would be costly.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B047 second. She notes Redding's role in quantitative and spatial follow-on work and asks whether the discovery's boundary overlaps with the quantitative trade literature.
responses.response: I agree with the concern about the boundary and have resolved it by excluding Redding from the preferred configuration. His contribution is important, but it is largely quantification and spatial extension of the core idea, and it is more recent. A tighter two-name prize keeps the citation on selection and heterogeneity and avoids absorbing the broader quantitative-trade programme, which a later committee could assess separately. Her point on Helpman's cross-listing also reinforces my choice not to combine B047 with B030.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B003 first, and his proposal includes Gertler alongside Kiyotaki and Moore. He treats the 2022 prize as related but not duplicative.
responses.response: I rank B003 third and think its core is the sharpest conceptual attribution on the shortlist: the 1997 Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism is clearly separable. I would keep it to the two originators. Gertler's strongest claim runs through the financial-accelerator lineage shared with Bernanke, who was recognised in 2022. That is the overlap I would not want to blur. B003 is my first alternative, and I would not oppose it if the Committee prefers cleaner attribution to B047's broader empirical record.

uncertainties: How to treat Bernard, Jensen, Eaton and Kortum, who are outside the credited names but have parallel or antecedent claims, and whether a Melitz-Helpman citation can be framed to avoid overstating priority.
How much weight the Committee gives to the Krugman 2008 overlap, and whether the selection-and-reallocation margin is seen as a distinct advance.
Where Helpman should be placed given the B030 cross-listing, and whether it is better to credit him with firm heterogeneity or with the political-economy-of-trade work.
Whether B047 can reach six votes given thinner top-three support than B014 or B003, and whether B003's cleaner attribution should take precedence.
My assessment relies on background knowledge of the literature and has not been independently verified against primary sources.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. My research is in economic history, covering regional growth, railways, electrification and historical national accounts. My listed co-authors are Lund economic-history colleagues, and none is a credited name on a shortlisted ballot entry. Tommy Andersson is a Lund colleague, but the profile shows no link to any shortlisted candidate.
